newsitem.title: USA: Stratton Oakmont brokers charged with perjury.
newsitem.headline: Stratton Oakmont brokers charged with perjury.

text.p: Two employees of the now-defunct investment banking firm Stratton Oakmont Inc were charged on Tuesday with stock fraud and perjury.

A complaint filed in Brooklyn Federal Court alleges that a manager/broker at the Long Island-based firm had an underling take two professional tests in his name and that both men lied to investigators about the identity-switching scheme.

The manager, a resident of of Coral Springs, Florida, had another broker sit in his place for both the Series 7 test required of all brokers who sell stocks to the general public, as well as the Series 24 test required of those in supervisory positions. Both exams are overseen by the National Association of Securities Dealers (NASD).
The case against the brokers arose out of NASD and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)'s investigation into the practices of Stratton Oakmont.

The firm was shut down by regulators in November after its brokers were found to have allegedly engaged in high pressure sales tactics and misleading clients. The company's assets were placed in bankruptcy court.

In April an NASD arbitration panel ordered four former Stratton Oakmont officers to pay $10 million in damages, the largest award ever in customer arbitration, to a Los Angeles doctor. The panel found a broker at the firm had given the man unsuitable investment information and made unauthorized transactions in his account.

Last year an SEC report also charged that the brokerage had allegedly broken its own rules of conduct when it gave preferential treatment to a high-profile client -- Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, a New York Republican.
The complaint filed in New York on Tuesday charged that the Florida broker used his ill-gotten licenses to sell about $30 million in stocks that made him $2 million richer.

Sources close to the investigation say the charges against the two ex-brokers were the first in a series that will be made by federal prosecutors in Brooklyn as they wrap up their probe of Stratton Oakmont.
